title: The woman at the well (John 4:1–42)
hookLine: at noon, alone, a Samaritan woman has the longest conversation with Jesus in the gospels

cards: About the sixth hour, John says: around noon, in the heat of the day. A woman comes alone, carrying her jar to Jacob's well outside a Samaritan town. John doesn't say why she came at that hour.
Maybe it was nothing. Some readers wonder if it was easier than facing the others. Sitting by the well, tired from the road, is a Jewish man she's never seen.
John adds a short note: Jews and Samaritans did not share things with each other. And the man looks up and speaks to her.

teach.b: He says, in the Douay-Rheims: "Give me to drink." She's startled. How is it that you, a Jew, ask a drink of me, a Samaritan woman?
He crossed two lines at once, and she noticed both. Then he turns it around: if you knew who was asking, you'd have asked him, and he'd have given you living water.
In Greek, living water also meant running water, fresh from a spring, as against a still cistern. She takes him literally: you have no bucket, and the well is deep. He goes further.
Whoever drinks this water will be thirsty again, but the water he gives becomes a spring inside, welling up to eternal life. Then he tells her to call her husband. She says she has none.
He tells her she's had five, and the man she has now isn't her husband. The Gospel never says why. Widowhood, divorce, a hard life: John is silent, and he never has Jesus condemn her.
She doesn't run. She asks a real question, about where God should be worshiped, this mountain or Jerusalem. He says the hour is coming when true worshipers will worship in spirit and in truth.

teach.h: SHE LEAVES THE JAR AND RUNS.
teach.b: Then she leaves her water jar and goes back into the town: "Come, and see a man who has told me all things whatsoever I have done."
And many believe because of her. In the East she's honored as a saint, called Photini, the enlightened one. Catholics hear her story in Lent, with those preparing for baptism at Easter.

how: Catholics read this Gospel on the Third Sunday of Lent in Year A, especially with those preparing for baptism at Easter; Eastern Christians honor the woman as Saint Photini.

John never says why she came at noon. readers wonder, but the text is silent.

games.q: you're the woman at the well. a stranger has just told you about your five husbands. what do you do?
o: pick up your jar and leave without a word.
ask him a real question about where to worship God.
tell him it's none of his business.
games.why: she keeps talking, and asks where God should be worshiped. then she leaves her jar and runs to tell the town.

practice: Notice that he spoke first, and asked for something, a drink: he let her give.

Think of one conversation that could be a little more honest than usual, not a confrontation, just true, like telling a friend how you really are, or asking a real question and waiting for the answer, and picture yourself at the well with that person, in no hurry.
If you pray, you can ask for the courage to say one true thing.

wordCard.voice: living water. What Jesus offered the Samaritan woman: a spring inside that wells up to eternal life, he said, for anyone who drinks it.

orig.note: Greek: living water, the everyday phrase for fresh running water from a spring.

carryVoice: Your line: he waited at the well. And she left her jar behind. Thirty-eight days now.
